Nearly every deep-learning *de novo* sequencing paper reports the same few
numbers: peptide recall, amino-acid precision and, more and more often, a curve
of precision against coverage. The names are the same from paper to paper; this
page checks whether the definitions are, twice over: against what {{n:n_read}} papers say they
computed, and against the evaluation code of {{n:n_impl}} implementations,
version by version.

**How it was done.** The papers are the catalog's {{n:n_papers}} deep-learning
method papers; {{n:n_unread}} of them could not be read in full and are left
out. Every metric a paper reports, with its definition
quoted and the section it came from, is in
[`papers.jsonl`](https://github.com/BioGeek/awesome_de_novo_peptide_sequencing/blob/main/analysis/metrics/papers.jsonl).
The code was read at the commit each row of the
[implementation table](#where-the-code-disagrees) links to, on 2026-11-22.
**Every number is a link** to an entry in
[Reproducing every number](#reproducing-every-number); the worked examples run
transcriptions of each tool's matching loop, and the entry names the file and
commit each was copied from.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Five things to know before putting two numbers side by side.**

1. **"Peptide precision" is usually a recall.** Scored against the search
   labels, precision is TP / (TP + FP): the predictions that match their label
   over the predictions made. Recall is TP / (TP + FN): the matches over all
   labelled spectra, a spectrum the model got wrong or left blank being a false
   negative. Casanovo's code calls its
   peptide figure `pep_precision` but divides by every labelled spectrum, which
   is the recall; NovoBench, denovo_benchmarks and PowerNovo2 do the same. The
   two agree only when the model predicts every spectrum
   ([why](#precision-recall-and-the-spectra-left-blank)).
   {{n:n_prec_named_recall}} papers define a "peptide precision" over all
   spectra; {{n:n_recall_named_prec}} define a "peptide recall" over predicted
   peptides only.
2. **Amino-acid precision and recall are swapped in a whole family of models.**
   Casanovo v3.0 to v3.5 passed the prediction where the label belonged, and
   v4.0 fixed it. The models that copied the v3 code did not:
   {{n:n_swapped_now}} entries in the table below still swap the two, among them
   ContraNovo, PrimeNovo, RefineNovo, RankNovo and π-HelixNovo. denovo_benchmarks
   swapped them from April 2024 to September 2026.
3. **The 0.1 Da mass rule counts some different residues as matches.** Under
   the matching rule DeepNovo introduced, which {{n:n_rule_mass}} of the papers
   state, K predicted for Q ({{n:d_kq}} Da apart), F for oxidised M
   ({{n:d_fm}} Da) and D for deamidated N ({{n:d_nd}} Da) count as matches, and
   so does a peptide containing them. ProteoBench's ppm tolerances and
   Casanovo-TMT's exact-peptidoform rule do not count them.
4. **"Peptide AUC" names at least three different areas.** NovoBench integrates
   precision against recall, which can never exceed the peptide recall; others
   integrate against coverage. For the same 1,000 predictions, half of them
   right and ranked first, the two give {{n:ex_auc_half_nb}} and {{n:ex_auc_half_cov}}.
5. **The "truth" is a search engine's answer.** The labels are database-search
   identifications accepted at a false discovery rate, typically 1%, so some of
   them are wrong, and only spectra a search could identify are labelled at all.
   Every figure here measures agreement with the search, not correctness.
:::

## What the papers report

{{n:n_pep}} of the {{n:n_read}} papers report a peptide-level figure, under one
name or another, {{n:n_aa}} report amino-acid precision or recall, and
{{n:n_curve}} a precision-coverage curve or the area under it. Fewer report an
FDR ({{n:n_fdr}}), PTM precision or recall ({{n:n_ptm}}) or calibration
({{n:n_calib}}), and {{n:n_new_metric}} introduce a metric of their own.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
papers_read = ns.papers.filter(d => d.read)
pub_href = slug => ["..", "publications", `${slug}.html`].join("/")
metric_counts = ns.groups
  .map(g => ({metric: g, n: papers_read.filter(d => d.reports.includes(g)).length}))
  .filter(d => d.n > 0)
  .sort((a, b) => b.n - a.n)
Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 860), height: 28 * metric_counts.length + 50,
  marginLeft: 200, marginRight: 50, marginBottom: 40,
  x: {label: `Papers (of ${papers_read.length} read)`, grid: true, labelOffset: 34},
  y: {label: null, domain: metric_counts.map(d => d.metric)},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(metric_counts, {x: "n", y: "metric", fill: "#2563eb", tip: true}),
    Plot.text(metric_counts, {x: "n", y: "metric", text: d => String(d.n), dx: 6, textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 11}),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
```

## The mass-matching rule

The rule was introduced with [DeepNovo](../algorithms/deepnovo.html) (2017). A
predicted residue counts as a **match** when its mass is within **0.1 Da** of the
label's residue and the prefix mass up to and including it is within **0.5 Da**
of the label's prefix. [Casanovo](../algorithms/casanovo.html) added a second pass from the
C-terminus, so a residue can also be matched on its suffix mass. A **peptide**
counts as a match when it has as many residues as the label and every one is
matched.

From those matches come the usual figures. **Amino-acid precision** divides the
matched residues by the predicted residues, **amino-acid recall** by the label's
residues. Sorting the predictions by the model's confidence and computing
precision at each depth gives **precision against coverage**.

### Precision, recall, and the spectra left blank

At peptide level, precision is TP / (TP + FP) and recall is TP / (TP + FN).
In practice the evaluation code scores each **labelled** spectrum against its
label, and counts it one of three ways:

- the model predicts the label's peptide: **counted as** a true positive;
- it predicts a different peptide: **counted as** a false positive, because it
  asserted something other than the label, and also as a false negative, because
  the label's peptide was not found;
- it predicts nothing, because it abstained, no candidate fitted the precursor
  mass, or the prediction fell below a confidence threshold: **counted as** a
  false negative only.

So **peptide precision** = matches / predictions made, and **peptide recall** =
matches / all labelled spectra. They differ only by the blanks. Take 100 labelled
spectra on which a model predicts 80 and matches the label on 60: precision is
{{n:ex_pep_prec}}, recall is {{n:ex_pep_rec}}. If it predicts all 100, both are
the share that matches.

"Counted as" is doing work there, because the label is a database-search
identification, not the peptide that produced the spectrum
([more below](#the-truth-is-a-search-engines-answer)). Two things the counting
cannot see:

- **A wrong label turns the counts around.** If the search mislabelled a
  spectrum and the model agrees with it, a false positive is counted as a true
  positive. If the model gets the real peptide, a true positive is counted as a
  false positive and a false negative. At a 1% FDR about one label in a hundred
  is expected to be wrong, and nothing in the evaluation says which.
- **Spectra the search did not identify are not counted at all.** The sample
  holds peptides that produced spectra but that the search missed: not in its
  database, carrying a modification it did not allow, or scoring below its
  threshold. They are in neither denominator. A model that sequences them
  correctly gains nothing, and a model that gets them wrong loses nothing. So
  "recall" is recall over what the search found, not over the peptides in the
  sample, and "precision" says nothing about the model's calls on the spectra
  *de novo* sequencing is most often used for.

Casanovo's `evaluate.py` returns a figure named `pep_precision` computed as
correct / all spectra passed to it. Since v4.0 every labelled spectrum is passed,
blanks included, so for the example above it prints {{n:ex_pep_rec}}: the recall.
Several papers call it "precision at coverage 1" (Pairwise, Modanovo), which is
accurate only when the model has predicted every spectrum; once it leaves some
blank, it is the recall. NovoBench, denovo_benchmarks and PowerNovo2 compute the same quantity
under the name "peptide precision", and so do the papers that use their code.
The reverse also happens: a few papers divide by the predictions made, which is
a precision, and call it recall.

Two things follow from matching on mass. I and L weigh the same, so they always
match, with no I/L rule needed. And so do pairs that differ by less than 0.1 Da:
under the rule, PEPTIDEQ counts as a match for PEPTIDEK ({{n:ex_kq_pep}} means
yes). [PepPr](../algorithms/peppr.html) points out that this makes deamidated N
equal to D and scores its deamidation calls on identity instead;
[Casanovo-TMT](../algorithms/casanovo-tmt.html) rejects the rule for the same
reason and requires the exact peptidoform. ProteoBench keeps the rule's shape but
in ppm: 20 ppm per residue and 50 ppm on the prefix. K and Q are
{{n:ppm_kq}} ppm apart, so there they count as different.

### The truth is a search engine's answer

Every one of these figures compares a prediction with a label, and the label is
not the peptide that produced the spectrum. It is the peptide a database search
assigned to it, kept if it passed a false discovery rate threshold, typically 1%.
That has three consequences for what "precision" and "recall" mean here.

- **Some labels are wrong.** At 1% FDR about one accepted identification in a
  hundred is expected to be false, and the FDR is itself an estimate from decoys,
  not a count. Where a *de novo* call disagrees with a wrong label, the call is
  scored as an error although it may be the right one. A perfect sequencer would
  not score 1, and two models that differ by less than the label error rate
  cannot be told apart on that evidence alone.
- **Only the identifiable spectra are labelled.** A spectrum enters the test set
  only if a search engine found a confident match in its database. That leaves out
  most of what *de novo* sequencing is for: peptides absent from the database,
  unexpected modifications, poor or chimeric spectra. Recall over labelled spectra
  says how well a model reproduces the search on the spectra the search could
  already do, not how it fares on the rest.
- **The labels carry the search's own choices.** Which engine, which database,
  which modifications were allowed and which threshold was applied all differ
  between benchmarks, and change between versions of the same benchmark: the
  [nine-species versions](nine-species-versions.html) relabel the same spectra
  differently. A search engine also cannot tell I from L, so neither can its labels.

So the field's "precision" and "recall" are agreement rates with a reference
that is itself uncertain. Precision in the strict sense, the share of
predictions that are right, cannot be measured on the unlabelled spectra at all,
which is why estimates of the error rate that need no search engine are now
appearing ([below](#error-rates-without-a-search-engine)).

### What the papers say about it

{{n:n_rule_mass}} papers state the 0.1 / 0.5 Da rule. {{n:n_rule_exact}} count a
residue or a peptide correct only on an exact sequence match, and
{{n:n_rule_other}} use a stricter mass rule or compare position by position:
[SMSNet](../algorithms/smsnet.html) wants the residue mass exact to 0.0001 Da and
the prefix within 0.03 Da, and PepNet and DPST compare position by position,
so one inserted residue makes everything after it wrong.
{{n:n_rule_none}} papers state no rule at all. On I and L, {{n:n_il_equal}} papers
say they count as equal and {{n:n_il_unstated}} do not say; that matters only
for the papers that compare strings.

The wording varies more than the rule. Most papers write that the prefix *or* the
suffix mass must agree; [RankNovo](../algorithms/ranknovo.html)'s text says both
must. Several measure a peptide as a string while measuring residues by mass, so
their peptide and amino-acid numbers rest on different definitions. And the names
do not follow the denominators: the table marks the {{n:n_prec_named_recall}}
papers that call a recall "precision" and the {{n:n_recall_named_prec}} that call
a precision "recall".

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
rule_order = ["0.1 / 0.5 Da mass rule", "Exact sequence", "Stricter mass rule", "Position by position", "Not stated"]
rule_counts = rule_order.map(r => ({rule: r, n: papers_read.filter(d => d.rule === r).length}))
Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 860), height: 28 * rule_counts.length + 50,
  marginLeft: 200, marginRight: 50, marginBottom: 40,
  x: {label: "Papers, by how they say a residue or peptide is matched", grid: true, labelOffset: 34},
  y: {label: null, domain: rule_order},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(rule_counts, {x: "n", y: "rule", fill: "#2563eb", tip: true}),
    Plot.text(rule_counts, {x: "n", y: "rule", text: d => String(d.n), dx: 6, textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 11}),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
  {placeholder: "Search the papers: method, metric, rule…"})
```

## Where the code disagrees

Nearly every implementation descends from one of two loops: DeepNovo's, which
walks forward only, and Casanovo's `evaluate.py`, which adds the pass from the
C-terminus. What separates the numbers is mostly not the rule but what happens
around it: which argument is the label, which spectra are counted, and which
version of the code ran.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof code_rows = Inputs.search(ns.code, {placeholder: "Search the implementations: tool, version, rule…"})
```

::: {.column-page}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
htl.html`<div class="wrap-table">${Inputs.table(code_rows, {
  columns: ["tool", "versions", "lineage", "rule", "order", "empty", "peptide", "curve", "url"],
  header: {tool: "Tool", versions: "Versions", lineage: "Copied from", rule: "Residue rule",
           order: "AA precision and recall", empty: "Spectra with no prediction",
           peptide: "Peptide figure", curve: "Curve or AUC", url: "Code"},
  format: {
    order: v => v === "swapped" ? htl.html`<strong>swapped</strong>` : v,
    url: (u, i, data) => htl.html`<a href="${u}" target="_blank" rel="noopener">${data[i].ref}</a>`
  },
  width: {tool: 140, versions: 105, lineage: 110, rule: 190, order: 85, empty: 160, peptide: 190, curve: 160, url: 70},
  layout: "fixed", height: 560
})}</div>`
```
:::

### Forward only, or forward and back

DeepNovo's loop walks both peptides from the N-terminus. When the prefix masses
drift apart by more than 0.5 Da, as they do after an inserted or wrong-mass
residue, nothing after the drift can match again. Casanovo's second pass from the
C-terminus recovers the residues after the error. Truth PEPTIDEK against the
prediction PEPGTIDEK matches {{n:ex_fwd}} residues forward only and
{{n:ex_best}} with Casanovo's rule. {{n:n_forward_only}} implementations in the
table are forward only: the DeepNovo family, GraphNovo, DIANovo, SMSNet, DiNovo
and [InstaNovo](../algorithms/instanovo.html), whose matcher carries an "adapted
from Casanovo" comment but is DeepNovo's loop. Their amino-acid numbers come out
lower on the same predictions; their peptide numbers do not change, because a
correct peptide never drifts.

### Precision and recall, swapped

Casanovo's `aa_match_batch` returns the residue counts in the order its two
peptide arguments came in, and `aa_match_metrics` expects the true count first.
From v3.0.0 to v3.5.0 the validation step passed the prediction first, so the
number printed as amino-acid precision was the recall and the other way round;
[commit 3a18fed](https://github.com/Noble-Lab/casanovo/commit/3a18fed) fixed it
for v4.0.0. For truth PEPTIDEK and prediction PEPTIDE, precision is
{{n:ex_swap_prec}} and recall {{n:ex_swap_rec}}; the swapped code prints
{{n:ex_swap_rec}} as precision. Peptide figures are unaffected, because the match
itself is symmetric.

Most of the models built on Casanovo v3 kept the swap, and their latest code
still has it: ContraNovo, PrimeNovo and every copy of it (π-PrimeNovo, ScopeNovo),
RefineNovo, RankNovo, DiffNovo, Transformer-DIA and DiffNovo-DIA, and every tag of
π-HelixNovo. TSARseqNovo copied the fixed v4.0 file and kept the old argument
order; pUniFind's own copy swaps them too. XuanjiNovo swapped them at its v1.1 tag
and has since fixed it, and π-MNovo fixed it in v0.2.0. The multi-tool benchmark
[denovo_benchmarks](https://github.com/bittremieuxlab/denovo_benchmarks) reversed
the arguments in April 2024 and fixed it on 26 September 2026
([commit 3a92eba](https://github.com/bittremieuxlab/denovo_benchmarks/commit/3a92eba)),
so its "AA precision" from that period is amino-acid recall.

### Which spectra are counted

Up to v3.5.0, Casanovo dropped every spectrum whose prediction was empty or
malformed from both sides of the comparison, so its peptide figure was computed
over the spectra that got a usable prediction, and a model that abstained more
scored higher. ContraNovo, the PrimeNovo family, RefineNovo, DiffNovo and
π-HelixNovo inherited that. From v4.0 Casanovo keeps them; NovoBench, AdaNovo and
dIon keep them too.

InstaNovo excludes empty predictions from precision only, which is what precision
means. But what counts as empty changed: before 1.2.0, beam search returned
nothing when no beam fitted the precursor mass, so precision was computed over
precursor-matched predictions only. From 1.2.0 those beams are kept, ranked after
the matching ones, so InstaNovo precision before and after 1.2.0 is not
like-for-like; the recall is. denovo_benchmarks made the opposite move on
8 February 2025: until then its "Pep precision" was correct over predicted
spectra, a precision, and from then on over all labelled spectra, a recall.

### One tool, several versions

**Casanovo.**

- v1.1 to v2.1 matched on the mass *before* each residue in a single pass.
- v3.0 rewrote that as the prefix-then-suffix rule used since.
- v3.0 to v3.5 swapped precision and recall and dropped empty predictions. v4.0
  fixed both, but in validation a spectrum whose beams were all discarded silently
  shifts the rest of its batch onto the wrong truth.
- v5.0 to v5.1.2: `casanovo sequence --evaluate` counted the padding of the true
  sequence as residues, so it printed a peptide precision of 0. v5.2.0 fixed it.
- v5: the validation code still splits a peptide before every capital letter, so
  `M[Oxidation]` becomes two pieces of mass 0, and any modified residue matches
  any other.
- The confidence that orders a precision-coverage curve changed three times: the
  mean of the residue scores minus 1 off-precursor (v3 to v4.3), the product minus
  1 (v5.0 to v5.1), and the product with no penalty (v5.2 on). The same model gives
  three different curves.

**InstaNovo.**

- 0.1.0 to 0.1.7 had the resynchronisation step inverted: after the first
  mismatch it advanced the peptide that was already ahead, so no later residue
  could match. GGPEPTIDE against NPEPTIDE matches {{n:ex_inv_01}} residues in 0.1.x
  and {{n:ex_inv_10}} from 1.0.0. Peptide figures were unaffected.
  [InstaNovo-P](../algorithms/instanovo-p.html) still ships the 0.1 step,
  including in its PTM matcher.
- 1.0.0 made its amino-acid error rate count I and L as equal; 0.1 counted every
  I/L call as an error.
- 1.2.0 changed which predictions are empty, as above.

**denovo_benchmarks** has had four evaluators: correct but over predicted spectra
only (March 2024), swapped (from April 2024), swapped and over all labelled
spectra (from February 2025), and correct over all labelled spectra (from
September 2026). **ProteoBench** stored no AUC until 4 August 2026, and has since
integrated precision against coverage at every distinct score.

### Smaller differences that still change a number

- **DeepNovo's peptide rule ignores the prediction's length**: a peptide counts as a
  match when every residue of the label is matched, so PEPTIDEK counts as a
  match for PEPTIDE. Its DIA and PointNovo descendants, given more than one candidate per
  spectrum, keep the candidate closest to the label; with the default of one it
  makes no difference.
- **DiffNovo** logs, per batch, the better of its two decoders, which no deployed
  system could choose, and its peptide slot holds an amino-acid value.
- **RankNovo** averages per-batch peptide recalls without weighting them by batch
  size, and weights the amino-acid figure by the first candidate's length.
- **MemNovo** strips every modification before matching and its mass table has no
  glycine, so a deleted G costs nothing; under its PrimeNovo model name it falls
  back to counting letters regardless of order.
- **PowerNovo2**'s precision-recall plot counts each correct residue as a negative
  as well, which caps the plotted precision at 0.5, and a results file holding any
  empty prediction is silently skipped.
- **PTM precision and recall** in NovoBench and AdaNovo inherit the mass rule, so F
  in place of an oxidised M counts toward PTM recall.
- **Unknown tokens** weigh 0 in Casanovo and its copies, so a label with an
  unparsed modification is scored with every later prefix mass off; InstaNovo and
  the DeepNovo family refuse it.

### Three areas called AUC

- **NovoBench** (and LIPNovo and SemiNovo, which copy it) integrates precision
  against recall: the area can never exceed the peptide recall, and wrong
  predictions add no width.
- **Precision against coverage**, coverage being the share of all spectra
  predicted, is what denovo_benchmarks (at 200 downsampled points), ProteoBench (at
  every distinct score), dIon and Casanovo's unreleased `dev` branch integrate. The
  Pairwise scripts compute coverage over predicted spectra only.
- **InstaNovo** integrates peptide precision against recall at 21 confidence
  quantiles.

On the same predictions the first two give {{n:ex_auc_half_nb}} and
{{n:ex_auc_half_cov}}; neither is wrong, but they are not the same number.

## Metrics beyond recall

### RankNovo's PMD and RMD

[RankNovo](../algorithms/ranknovo.html) reranks the candidates of several
sequencers, and to train the reranker it introduced two measures of how far a
candidate is from the label. Both are training targets, not evaluation metrics:
the paper still reports peptide recall and amino-acid precision, and the released
code computes those with the swapped Casanovo v3 call.

**PMD, Peptide Mass Deviation**, is an edit distance in which inserting or
deleting a residue costs one unit and substituting one costs the mass difference;
the released code fixes the unit at 51.4238 Da. It is not the difference between
the two peptides' masses: GG against N, which weigh the same, costs
{{n:pmd_gg_n}} units, a missing residue costs {{n:pmd_del}} unit whatever it
weighs, and K for Q costs {{n:pmd_kq}}.

**RMD, Residual Mass Deviation**, gives each residue of the candidate the signed
offset between its prefix mass and the nearest prefix mass of the label. For
PEPGGK against PEPNK it is {{n:rmd_gg_mid}} Da at the first G and
{{n:rmd_gg_last}} Da at the end, where the masses agree again. In the released
inference code only the PMD head chooses the candidate; the RMD head is computed
and discarded. No other repository implements either.

### Error rates without a search engine

A recall needs labels, which only database search provides, so the field has
started to estimate error rates on unlabelled spectra:
[Winnow](../algorithms/winnow.html) turns calibrated confidence into an FDR (the
mean of one minus the confidence above a threshold);
[DiNovo](../algorithms/dinovo.html) maps predictions to a target-decoy protein
database; π-NovoQC compares counterpart spectra; Casanovo's 2023 preprint and
[Casanovo-TMT](../algorithms/casanovo-tmt.html) count matches to a shuffled or
decoy digest, the latter saying plainly that this is not a search-engine FDR; and
[Cascadia](../algorithms/cascadia.html) counts a DIA prediction correct when it
matches the reference proteome exactly.

### Other measures

Casanovo 5 reports a calibration curve. [DiffuNovo](../algorithms/diffunovo.html)
reports the error of the predicted peptide's mass and the share within 0.001 Da.
[BiATNovo](../algorithms/biatnovo.html) adds a position-weighted BLEU and a
mass-aware alignment score, the QuasiNovo thesis a longest common subsequence
anchored on terminal masses, OmniNovo backbone and modification-site accuracy,
Spectralis precision and recall of its fragment-bin corrections, and NovoCRF recall
split by how much fragment-ion evidence each spectrum holds.

## Reading a number

Before comparing two published figures, find out:

1. **Which code, at which version**, computed it. A Casanovo v3 descendant and a
   Casanovo v4 one print the same labels for different quantities.
2. **The denominator.** All labelled spectra, spectra with a prediction, or
   spectra with a well-formed prediction.
3. **The residue rule.** The 0.1 / 0.5 Da mass rule, ppm, or an exact sequence.
4. **For a curve, which confidence orders it, and what the area is taken
   against.**

{{appendix}}
